name: FLOW-MATIC
code:
(0) INPUT WORDS FILE-A ; OUTPUT LISTING FILE-B ; HSP B .
(1) X-1 SET NUMBER (W) , COUNT-3 (W) AND COUNT-5 (W) TO ZERO .
(2) X-1 ADD ONE TO NUMBER (W) , COUNT-3 (W) AND COUNT-5 (W) .
(3) TEST COUNT-3 (W) AGAINST 3 ; IF EQUAL GO TO OPERATION 10 ;
    OTHERWISE GO TO OPERATION 4 .
(4) TEST COUNT-5 (W) AGAINST 5 ; IF EQUAL GO TO OPERATION 7 ;
    OTHERWISE GO TO OPERATION 5 .
(5) MOVE NUMBER (W) TO LINE (B) .
(6) JUMP TO OPERATION 16 .
(7) X-1 SET COUNT-5 (W) TO ZERO .
(8) MOVE BUZZ (A) TO LINE (B) .
(9) JUMP TO OPERATION 16 .
(10) X-1 SET COUNT-3 (W) TO ZERO .
(11) TEST COUNT-5 (W) AGAINST 5 ; IF EQUAL GO TO OPERATION 14 ;
    OTHERWISE GO TO OPERATION 12 .
(12) MOVE FIZZ (A) TO LINE (B) .
(13) JUMP TO OPERATION 16 .
(14) X-1 SET COUNT-5 (W) TO ZERO .
(15) MOVE FIZZBUZZ (A) TO LINE (B) .
(16) WRITE-ITEM B .
(17) TEST NUMBER (W) AGAINST 100 ; IF EQUAL GO TO OPERATION 18 ;
    OTHERWISE GO TO OPERATION 2 .
(18) READ-ITEM A ; IF END OF DATA GO TO OPERATION 19 .
(19) CLOSE-OUT FILES B .
(20) STOP . (END)
checked_with: Every FLOW-MATIC operation (INPUT, TEST, MOVE, JUMP, WRITE-ITEM, READ-ITEM, CLOSE-OUT, STOP, and the X-1 entry form) checked against the 1958 UNIVAC manual U1518. Not confirmed: the UNIVAC machine code inside the X-1 sections (not written), the data designs, and how a numeric test value is written for a short field. The flow of operations was traced in Python.
note: The 1958 manual lists no verb for arithmetic: adding or multiplying was done in X-1 sections of hand-written UNIVAC machine code, as the manual's own sample problem does, so the counting here is done that way and only the comparisons, moves and jumps are FLOW-MATIC. The words come from a one-item input file, and numbers would print with leading zeros.

name: COBOL
code:
IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.
       PROGRAM-ID. FIZZBUZZ.
       DATA DIVISION.
       WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
       01  N        PIC 999.
       01  N-SHOWN  PIC ZZ9.
       PROCEDURE DIVISION.
           PERFORM VARYING N FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL N > 100
               EVALUATE TRUE
                   WHEN FUNCTION MOD(N, 15) = 0
                       DISPLAY "FizzBuzz"
                   WHEN FUNCTION MOD(N, 3) = 0
                       DISPLAY "Fizz"
                   WHEN FUNCTION MOD(N, 5) = 0
                       DISPLAY "Buzz"
                   WHEN OTHER
                       MOVE N TO N-SHOWN
                       DISPLAY FUNCTION TRIM(N-SHOWN)
               END-EVALUATE
           END-PERFORM
           STOP RUN.
checked_with: Fixed format, GnuCOBOL-compatible. PERFORM VARYING, EVALUATE TRUE, FUNCTION MOD, FUNCTION TRIM, DISPLAY and the PIC ZZ9 edited item checked against the GnuCOBOL Programmer's Guide. No COBOL compiler was available to run it.
note: The number is moved into an edited picture, ZZ9, which blanks leading zeros, and TRIM removes the blanks before it is shown. Code starts in column 8, as fixed format requires.

name: SQL
code:
WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n) AS (
    SELECT 1
    UNION ALL
    SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 100
)
SELECT CASE
           WHEN n % 15 = 0 THEN 'FizzBuzz'
           WHEN n % 3 = 0 THEN 'Fizz'
           WHEN n % 5 = 0 THEN 'Buzz'
           ELSE CAST(n AS TEXT)
       END AS result
FROM numbers
ORDER BY n;
checked_with: Run with sqlite3 3.49.1 (Python's sqlite3); output matched FizzBuzz exactly.
note: Written in SQLite's dialect: a recursive common table expression makes the numbers 1 to 100, and CASE picks the word. The % operator works in SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL; standard SQL spells it MOD(n, 15).

name: Natural
code:
DEFINE DATA LOCAL
1 #N  (I2)
1 #Q  (I2)
1 #R3 (I2)
1 #R5 (I2)
END-DEFINE
*
FOR #N 1 TO 100
  DIVIDE 3 INTO #N GIVING #Q REMAINDER #R3
  DIVIDE 5 INTO #N GIVING #Q REMAINDER #R5
  DECIDE FOR FIRST CONDITION
    WHEN #R3 = 0 AND #R5 = 0
      WRITE NOTITLE 'FizzBuzz'
    WHEN #R3 = 0
      WRITE 'Fizz'
    WHEN #R5 = 0
      WRITE 'Buzz'
    WHEN NONE
      WRITE #N
  END-DECIDE
END-FOR
*
END
checked_with: Structured mode. DEFINE DATA, FOR, DIVIDE ... GIVING ... REMAINDER, DECIDE FOR FIRST CONDITION and WRITE NOTITLE checked against the Natural 8.2.7 statements reference (read from the Internet Archive's copies; the live pages now return 404). The WRITE page says that if NOTITLE is used it applies to all DISPLAY, PRINT and WRITE statements within the same object that write to the same report, and its FOR and DIVIDE examples put NOTITLE on one WRITE only. Not run.
note: Natural has a DIVIDE statement that gives a remainder, so each number is divided twice before a DECIDE chooses the word. NOTITLE, written once, stops Natural adding its usual page title to the whole report, and numbers are written right-aligned in their field, as in any Natural report.

name: HyperTalk
code:
on mouseUp
  put empty into fizzBuzz
  repeat with n = 1 to 100
    put empty into thisLine
    if n mod 3 is 0 then put "Fizz" after thisLine
    if n mod 5 is 0 then put "Buzz" after thisLine
    if thisLine is empty then put n into thisLine
    put thisLine & return after fizzBuzz
  end repeat
  put fizzBuzz into card field "Output"
end mouseUp
checked_with: on mouseUp, repeat with, mod, one-line if ... then, put ... into/after, empty, & return and card field checked against Goodman's HyperTalk Bible (1989) and Apple's HyperTalk Beginner's Guide (1989). No HyperCard to run it.
note: HyperTalk has no console, so the script runs when a button is clicked and puts the lines into a field on the card. Each line is built by putting words after it, which reads close to English.

name: AppleScript

set theLines to ""
repeat with n from 1 to 100
    if n mod 15 is 0 then
        set theLines to theLines & "FizzBuzz" & linefeed
    else if n mod 3 is 0 then
        set theLines to theLines & "Fizz" & linefeed

theLines

note: Joining a number onto text turns the number into text, because the text is on the left. The script's last line is its result, which Script Editor and osascript display.

name: Inform 7
checked_with: repeat with ... running from ... to, remainder after dividing ... by, if / otherwise if / otherwise, say with [N] and [line break], To phrases and When play begins checked against Writing with Inform and the Basic Inform phrase definitions. Not compiled.
note: Inform needs a room before it will compile, so the story has one, and the lines are printed when play begins, before the game's banner. Blocks are indented with tabs, which Inform reads as its indentation.

name: Osmosian Plain English
code:
To run:
  Start up.
  Loop.
  If a counter is past 100, break.
  If the counter is evenly divisible by 15, write "FizzBuzz"; repeat.
  If the counter is evenly divisible by 3, write "Fizz"; repeat.
  If the counter is evenly divisible by 5, write "Buzz"; repeat.
  Convert the counter to a string.
  Write the string.
  Repeat.
  Wait for the escape key.
  Shut down.
checked_with: To run:, Start up., Loop. / Repeat. / break, If a counter is past ..., is evenly divisible by, one-line conditionals with semicolons, Convert ... to a string and Write checked against the Osmosian instructions. Not in the instructions: Wait for the escape key, which is taken from the language's published Hello World. Not run (the compiler is Windows-only and was not installed).
note: "If a counter is past 100" both adds one to a new local counter and tests it, so the loop needs no separate counting step. Every conditional fits on one line, as the language requires.

name: Attempto Controlled English
code:
If there is a number N and there is a number K and there is an integer M and N = K * M then N is a multiple of K.
If a number N is a multiple of 3 and N is a multiple of 5 then the output of N is "FizzBuzz".
If a number N is a multiple of 3 and N is not a multiple of 5 then the output of N is "Fizz".
If a number N is a multiple of 5 and N is not a multiple of 3 then the output of N is "Buzz".
If a number N is not a multiple of 3 and N is not a multiple of 5 then the output of N is N.
If there is an integer N and N >= 1 and N =< 100 then a program prints the output of N.
checked_with: Variables in apposition, if ... then, is not, of-phrases, strings, integers, arithmetic with * and boolean formulas such as N =< 100 checked against the ACE construction rules. Not parsed with APE, which was not available locally; the content words (multiple, output, program, prints) rely on APE's lexicon.
note: ACE has + - * / but no remainder, so "multiple" is defined with a multiplication. These sentences state the rules as logic; they do not run, and they say nothing about the order in which the lines appear.

name: PENG
code: No sample is given. PENG's published papers show conditionals, universal quantifiers, negation and comparatives over user-defined words, but no arithmetic, no remainder and no output, so a FizzBuzz written in PENG would be invented rather than checked.
checked_with: Schwitter's PENG papers (2002, 2003, 2006) and the PENG Light paper (2009) were read. None shows numbers used as values, arithmetic, a remainder or any output.
note: There is too little published about PENG's grammar to write FizzBuzz in it faithfully. Its editor offers only the words that may come next, so the sentences a writer can type depend on a lexicon that is not published.

name: SBVR Structured English
code:
It is obligatory that each integer that is greater than 0 and that is less than 101 is printed.
It is obligatory that each integer that is a multiple of 3 and that is a multiple of 5 is printed as 'FizzBuzz'.
It is obligatory that each integer that is a multiple of 3 and that is not a multiple of 5 is printed as 'Fizz'.
It is obligatory that each integer that is a multiple of 5 and that is not a multiple of 3 is printed as 'Buzz'.
It is obligatory that each integer that is not a multiple of 3 and that is not a multiple of 5 is printed as the numeral of the integer.
checked_with: The rule form (It is obligatory that each ... that ...), the keywords each, that, and, not, and the quoted names checked against the OMG SBVR 1.5 specification. The verbs (is greater than, is a multiple of, is printed as) would have to be defined in the business vocabulary.
note: These are business rules: each says what must be true, not how to make it so, and nothing here runs. In the specification, terms, verbs, names and keywords are told apart by font and colour, which plain text loses, and rules cannot say what order the lines come in.

name: Gherkin
code:
Feature: FizzBuzz
  Each number from 1 to 100 is said as itself,
  except that multiples of 3 are said as "Fizz",
  multiples of 5 as "Buzz", and multiples of both as "FizzBuzz".

  Scenario Outline: Saying a number
    When I say the number <number>
    Then I hear "<words>"

    Examples:
      | number | words    |
      | 1      | 1        |
      | 2      | 2        |
      | 3      | Fizz     |
      | 5      | Buzz     |
      | 6      | Fizz     |
      | 10     | Buzz     |
      | 15     | FizzBuzz |
      | 98     | 98       |
      | 99     | Fizz     |
      | 100    | Buzz     |

note: The feature file states examples of the behaviour; to run it, a programmer must write a step definition for each of the two step patterns, in a language such as Java, JavaScript or Ruby, plus the FizzBuzz code they call. It checks the ten numbers in the table, not all hundred.

name: Quorum

repeat while n <= 100
    if n mod 15 = 0
        output "FizzBuzz"

name: Hedy
checked_with: Level 14. Transpiled with Hedy's own transpiler, hedylang 0.0.11 (the version pinned in Hedy's requirements-prod.txt), and run with Hedy's runtime prefix; output matched FizzBuzz exactly. Hedy pauses 0.1 s per loop pass, which was switched off for the run. The level 14 transpiler turns range(1, 100) into Python's range(1, 100 + step, step), so 100 is included.
note: Hedy's level 14 grammar has no remainder operator, and its documentation shows none at any level, so the program keeps two counters and resets them. At level 14 an if may have only one elif, so the Buzz case is a nested if.

name: Jac

name: Jac with by llm
checked_with: Passes jac check with jaclang 0.16.7 (warnings only, because the byllm plugin could not be installed here). Syntax checked against the by llm reference and jaclang's bundled jac-by-llm guide, which says to describe the function with sem, not a docstring. No model was called.

name: DSPy
code:
import dspy

dspy.configure(lm=dspy.LM("openai/gpt-4o-mini"))


class FizzBuzz(dspy.Signature):
    """Say what FizzBuzz says for a number: Fizz for a multiple of 3,
    Buzz for a multiple of 5, FizzBuzz for a multiple of both,
    and otherwise the number itself."""

    number: int = dspy.InputField()
    says: str = dspy.OutputField()


fizzbuzz = dspy.Predict(FizzBuzz)

for n in range(1, 101):
    print(fizzbuzz(number=n).says)
checked_with: Signature, InputField, OutputField, Predict and dspy.LM checked against the DSPy signatures guide, and the program run end to end with dspy 3.5.0 and its DummyLM, which returns canned answers, to confirm the API. No real model was called.
note: The signature's docstring and field names become the prompt, and a model fills in says for each number. DSPy could tune the prompt against a metric, but each answer is still the model's guess.

note: The function is a typed prompt; the host program would call it once per number. The test can assert that 15 gives FizzBuzz, but only by asking the model, so it can pass one day and fail the next.

name: Marsha
code:
# func fizzbuzz(integer): string

This function takes a whole number and returns what is said for it in FizzBuzz: 'Fizz' if the number is a multiple of 3, 'Buzz' if it is a multiple of 5, 'FizzBuzz' if it is a multiple of both, and otherwise the number written in digits.

* fizzbuzz(1) = '1'
* fizzbuzz(3) = 'Fizz'
* fizzbuzz(5) = 'Buzz'
* fizzbuzz(15) = 'FizzBuzz'
* fizzbuzz(98) = '98'
* fizzbuzz(0) throws an error
checked_with: The # func header, integer and string types, the description and the * example lines checked against Marsha's README and its fibonacci and roman_numerals examples. Not compiled, since compiling calls a model.
note: Marsha asks a model to write Python from the description and turns the examples into tests that the Python must pass. The answer is then computed by that generated Python, which is only as right as the five examples make it.

name: Jev
checked_with: TypeSafeClient, system_one, Choice with instructions and criteria, and response.choices[...].choice checked against TypeSafe's quickstart and Choice pages. No request was sent.
note: Jev writes no text and does no arithmetic: it gives a probability to each of four listed answers, so this sends a hundred requests to guess what one line of remainder arithmetic would compute exactly. It is the wrong tool for FizzBuzz, and its documentation says to keep questions simple and do the rest in code.

name: Instructor
code:
from typing import Literal

import instructor
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class Line(BaseModel):
    number: int
    says: Literal["Fizz", "Buzz", "FizzBuzz"] | int


class FizzBuzz(BaseModel):
    lines: list[Line] = Field(min_length=100, max_length=100)


client = instructor.from_provider("openai/gpt-4o-mini")

result = client.create(
    response_model=FizzBuzz,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Play FizzBuzz for the numbers 1 to 100."}],
    max_retries=3,
)

for line in result.lines:
    print(line.says)
checked_with: from_provider and create(response_model=..., messages=..., max_retries=...) checked against the Instructor docs and the signatures in instructor 1.17.0. The Pydantic response model was tested locally: it accepts a correct answer, rejects 99 lines, and accepts a wrong answer. No model was called.
note: Pydantic checks that there are exactly a hundred lines and that each is a number or one of the three words, and Instructor asks again when it fails. A reply with Fizz in the wrong place passes.

name: Outlines
code:
from typing import Literal

import outlines
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

MODEL_NAME = "microsoft/Phi-4-mini-instruct"
model = outlines.from_transformers(
    AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME, device_map="auto"),
    AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME),
)

for n in range(1, 101):
    answer = model(
        "In FizzBuzz, multiples of 3 are Fizz, multiples of 5 are Buzz, "
        "multiples of both are FizzBuzz, and other numbers are said as they are. "
        f"What is said for {n}?",
        Literal["Fizz", "Buzz", "FizzBuzz", str(n)],
    )
    print(answer)
checked_with: from_transformers and model(prompt, output_type) with a Literal type checked against the Outlines README (version 1 API). A Literal built from str(n) at run time is ordinary Python but is not shown in the docs. Not run.
note: Generation is constrained to the four allowed answers for each number, so the shape is guaranteed. The arithmetic is not: the model may still say Fizz for 5.

name: Guidance
code:
from guidance import select
from guidance.models import Transformers

lm = Transformers("microsoft/Phi-4-mini-instruct")
lm += (
    "In FizzBuzz, multiples of 3 are Fizz, multiples of 5 are Buzz, "
    "multiples of both are FizzBuzz, and other numbers are said as they are.\n"
)
for n in range(1, 101):
    lm += f"{n}: "
    lm += select(["Fizz", "Buzz", "FizzBuzz", str(n)], name="says")
    lm += "\n"
    print(lm["says"])
checked_with: models.Transformers, lm += text, select([...], name=...) and lm[name] checked against the Guidance README. Guidance could not be installed here, so it was not imported. Not run.
note: select forces each line to be one of four strings, so the shape is guaranteed while the model writes. Which string it selects is the model's arithmetic, and is not guaranteed.

name: NaturalJava
code:
Create a for loop that iterates from 1 to 100.
Declare a String called word and initialize it to "".
Create an if statement controlled by i mod 3 equals 0.
Assign word plus "Fizz" to word.
Leave this if statement.
Create an if statement controlled by i mod 5 equals 0.
Assign word plus "Buzz" to word.
Leave this if statement.
Create an if statement controlled by word's isEmpty.
Assign word plus i to word.
Leave this if statement.
Call System.out's println and pass it word.
checked_with: The paper shows the wording of the for-loop command, declarations, if statements, "Assign x plus y to z", method calls ("Call ... and pass it ...") and "Leave this loop". It shows no remainder, no printing, no else and no Java for a for loop, so those commands are extrapolated and the Java it would produce is not given.
note: NaturalJava builds a Java program from one typed request at a time, each holding a single action, which is why FizzBuzz becomes a dozen commands. The loop variable is assumed to be i, since the paper does not show the Java a for loop becomes.

name: Metafor
code: There is a game with a player who counts from 1 to 100. Each time the player reaches a number, the player says it. If the number can be divided by 3 and by 5, the player says "FizzBuzz" instead; otherwise, if it can be divided by 3, the player says "Fizz"; otherwise, if it can be divided by 5, the player says "Buzz".
checked_with: Read the IUI 2005 and CHI 2005 papers. They show stories becoming Python-like scaffolding (classes, methods, if/else from "if ...; otherwise"), and say that people describe sets rather than loops. They show no counted loop, no arithmetic beyond a comparison and no printing, so what Metafor would produce from this story is not given.
note: Metafor reads a story and drafts code to be finished by a programmer; its authors say the output may not run. A player who "says" something would become a method call on the player, not a print statement.

name: Pegasus
code: The paper could not be read for this page, so no sample is given.
checked_with: The Onward! 2006 paper could not be obtained (ACM returned 403; no open copy was found). The project's own site was read; it gives examples, including "which can be divided by 3", but describes most of them as what Pegasus will be able to do.
